title: Slow Down And Be A Better, Calmer Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the assumption that a packed curriculum and overloaded schedule force teachers to rush, arguing instead that slowing down actually makes a teacher more effective, not less. He lists concrete benefits of a slower pace -- better decision-making, more observational time, clearer thinking, better rapport -- then breaks down seven specific areas where small adjustments recover time: building routines for anything students can do independently, narrowing lessons to a single objective and cutting at least 25 percent of teaching time, holding true independence during work time, using visualization to mentally rehearse the day, cutting a third of overall talking, and consciously deepening one's breathing. His underlying argument is that most of a teacher's perceived time pressure is self-created through unnecessary talking, over-broad lessons, and unnecessary hand-holding, and that eliminating these habits creates genuine slack rather than requiring more hours in the day.
points: Teachers should challenge themselves to cut at least 25 percent of current lesson time by narrowing each lesson to a single objective.
A concrete goal is to eliminate a third of overall teacher talking, since most time pressure is self-created through unnecessary explanation.
Diaphragmatic breathing, focused on the exhale, is offered as a physiological lever that stimulates the parasympathetic nervous system and lowers blood pressure.
Building routines for anything students can already do independently is the single biggest recovered-time category Linsin observes when visiting classrooms.
Calm energy transfers from teacher to class automatically, meaning slowing down is itself a behavior management intervention, not just a personal wellness tip.
quotes: In fact, being in a hurry means that you’re far less effective than you could be if you just slowed down.
Nearly every time I visit a classroom, the teacher spends countless minutes talking students through transitions and instructions that students can fully handle on their own.
Challenge yourself to cut at least 25 percent from the current time it takes you to teach each lesson.
Most teachers could stand to cut at least a third of the amount of talking they do.
By breathing through your nose, filling your diaphragm, and focusing on your exhale, you stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system.
The best news is that by slowing down, your calm energy will fill your classroom and soothe and focus your class.
